answer_text:
We need the residue of

\[
f(z)=\frac{(z+2\pi)^3\cos z}{1-\sin(3z)}
\]

at

\[
z=\frac{\pi}{3}.
\]

A residue is nonzero only if the point is a singularity of the function. So first check whether \(z=\frac{\pi}{3}\) makes the denominator zero.

The denominator vanishes when

\[
1-\sin(3z)=0
\]

or

\[
\sin(3z)=1.
\]

This occurs when

\[
3z=\frac{\pi}{2}+2\pi k,
\]

so

\[
z=\frac{\pi}{6}+\frac{2\pi k}{3}, \qquad k\in\mathbb{Z}.
\]

Now test whether \(z=\frac{\pi}{3}\) is among these points:

\[
\frac{\pi}{3} \neq \frac{\pi}{6}+\frac{2\pi k}{3}
\]

for any integer \(k\). Indeed, substituting \(z=\frac{\pi}{3}\),

\[
\sin(3z)=\sin(\pi)=0,
\]

so

\[
1-\sin(3z)=1-0=1\neq 0.
\]

Thus the function is analytic at \(z=\frac{\pi}{3}\). Therefore its Laurent expansion about that point has no negative-power terms, and the residue is

\[
\boxed{0}.
\]

27B·v4.method: Verify denominator is nonzero at z=π/3, concluding the function is analytic and residue is 0.
